title: Plusquamperfekt (Past of the past)
bridge: In Spanish, we use the pluperfect (había comido) to express an action that occurred before another in the past. In German, the Plusquamperfekt (hatte gegessen) works in a very similar way, but it is formed with the auxiliary verbs 'haben' or 'sein' in the preterite (Präteritum) and the past participle at the end of the sentence. A key difference is that in German, the auxiliary appears in second position in main clauses, and in subordinate clauses the auxiliary is placed at the end, which can be confusing. Additionally, the Plusquamperfekt is often used with 'nachdem' (after) to indicate anteriority, whereas in Spanish the simple past (pretérito perfecto simple) is sometimes used.
rule: The Plusquamperfekt is formed with the preterite of 'haben' (hatte, hattest, hatte, hatten, hattet, hatten) or 'sein' (war, warst, war, waren, wart, waren) + the past participle (Partizip II) of the main verb, usually at the end of the sentence. 'Sein' is used for verbs indicating movement or a change of state without an accusative object, such as 'gehen', 'kommen', 'fahren', 'bleiben', 'sein', etc. For most other verbs, 'haben' is used. In main clauses, the conjugated auxiliary occupies the second position; in subordinate clauses (with 'nachdem', 'weil', etc.), the auxiliary goes at the end. Examples: 'Ich hatte das Buch gelesen' (I had read the book) and 'Sie war nach Berlin gefahren' (She had gone to Berlin). The Plusquamperfekt is commonly used with 'nachdem' to express a fully completed action before another in the past, or in narratives to indicate anteriority. It is also used in indirect speech or formal contexts. To form the Partizip II: regular verbs with the prefix 'ge-' and ending '-t' (e.g. 'gemacht'), irregular verbs with vowel changes and ending '-en' (e.g. 'gegangen'), separable verbs with the prefix at the beginning (e.g. 'aufgemacht'), and non-separable verbs without 'ge-' (e.g. 'verstanden'). Remember the verbs with 'haben' and 'sein' as auxiliaries: 'haben' for transitive and reflexive verbs, 'sein' for intransitive verbs of movement or change.

title: Konditionalsätze Typ 1 und 2 / Conditional sentences type 1 and 2
bridge: In Spanish, we use the subjunctive to express hypothetical conditions (si tuviera, si hubiera). In German, the Konjunktiv II (a form similar to the subjunctive) is used in type 2 conditional sentences, but in type 1, the present indicative is used in both clauses, which can be surprising for Spanish speakers. Additionally, in German the conjunction 'wenn' introduces the condition, and the conjugated verb goes at the end of that clause, whereas in Spanish the word order is more flexible. Caution: do not use the Konjunktiv II in type 1, as it would change the meaning to improbable.
rule: Conditional sentences express a condition and its consequence. Type 1 (real or possible): formed with 'wenn' + present indicative in the conditional clause, and present or future in the main clause. Structure: 'Wenn ich Zeit habe, gehe ich ins Kino' (If I have time, I go to the cinema). The conjugated verb in the clause with 'wenn' goes at the end. In the main clause, the verb goes in second position. Type 2 (unreal or hypothetical): formed with 'wenn' + Konjunktiv II (past subjunctive). For regular verbs, 'würde' + infinitive is used; for modal verbs and some irregular verbs, their own form is used (e.g. hätte, wäre, könnte). Structure: 'Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich ins Kino gehen' (If I had time, I would go to the cinema). The order can also be reversed: the main clause can come first, followed by the conditional clause. In that case, the main clause has the verb in second position and the conditional clause begins with 'wenn'. It is common to use 'dann' at the beginning of the main clause when the conditional clause comes first.

title: Das Passiv (Präsens und Präteritum) / Passive voice (present and past tense)
bridge: In Spanish, the passive voice is formed with 'ser' + past participle, and the agent is introduced with 'por'. In German, 'werden' + Partizip II is also used, but there are key differences: the agent is introduced with 'von' (for people) or 'durch' (for things or means), and the participle goes at the end of the sentence. Additionally, German often prefers the active voice or constructions with 'man' (one) instead of the passive, so don’t overuse it. Be careful: don’t confuse 'werden' (for passive) with 'sein' (state).
rule: The passive voice in German is formed with the auxiliary verb 'werden' (conjugated) + the Partizip II of the main verb, which is placed at the end of the sentence. In the present tense: 'werden' is conjugated as: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie werden. In the past tense (Präteritum): ich wurde, du wurdest, er/sie/es wurde, wir wurden, ihr wurdet, sie wurden. The agent (who performs the action) is introduced with 'von' + dative if it is a person or institution, and with 'durch' + accusative if it is a means or instrument. If the agent is not mentioned, it is omitted. Examples: 'Das Haus wird gebaut' (The house is being built). In the past: 'Das Haus wurde gebaut' (The house was built). Exception: modal verbs in passive: 'Das muss gemacht werden' (That must be done). To express a resulting state, 'sein' + Partizip II is used: 'Das Haus ist gebaut' (The house is built). Typical use: in news, reports, and when the agent is unknown or irrelevant. Unlike Spanish, there is no common reflexive passive ('se'); instead, 'man' is used in the active voice or the passive with 'werden'.

title: Indirect Speech (Basic indirect style) / Indirekte Rede (Grundlegende indirekte Rede)
bridge: In Spanish, when shifting from direct to indirect speech, the verb tense changes (dijo: "voy" → dijo que iba). In German, the tense shift is more flexible, and sometimes the same tense is maintained. The key is to use the subjunctive I (Konjunktiv I) to indicate an indirect quote, whereas in Spanish the subjunctive or indicative is used depending on the context. A typical error is confusing subjunctive I with subjunctive II or using the indicative as in Spanish.
rule: In German, indirect speech (indirekte Rede) is used to report what someone has said, thought, or written. The main verb is usually 'sagen' (to say), 'erzählen' (to tell), 'erklären' (to explain), or similar. The most common form at B1 level is the Konjunktiv I, which is formed from the present tense stem: for most verbs, it is the same as the present tense in all persons except the 3rd person singular, which matches the 1st person singular. Example: 'er sagt' → 'er sage'. For verbs whose Konjunktiv I is identical to the indicative (such as in the 1st or 3rd person plural), the Konjunktiv II (würde + infinitive) is used to avoid ambiguity. The indicative can also be used if the quote is obvious, but at B1 level, Konjunktiv I is preferred. The main connector is 'dass' (that) or the structure without 'dass' can be used with the verb in second position (inversion).

title: Infinitiv und Gerundium / Infinitives and gerunds as subject and object
bridge: In Spanish, we use the infinitive (hablar) and the gerund (hablando) clearly: the gerund usually expresses actions in progress. In German, the gerund (the form ending in -ndo) does not exist as such; instead, the infinitive with 'zu' or nominalized constructions are mainly used. This can confuse you when translating directly: where in Spanish you say 'Me gusta nadar', in German it is 'Ich mag Schwimmen' (noun) or 'Ich schwimme gern' (conjugated verb). To talk about activities as subjects or objects, German prefers the infinitive with 'zu' or the verb-derived noun.
rule: In German, the infinitive can be used as a noun (das Schwimmen, das Lesen) when it acts as a subject. To express 'me gusta + verb', 'gern' is used with the conjugated verb, not a gerund. When one verb follows another, the infinitive with 'zu' is used (Ich hoffe, dich zu sehen) or without 'zu' if the first verb is modal (Ich kann schwimmen). Some verbs like 'gehen', 'bleiben' or 'lernen' can be combined with the infinitive without 'zu' (Ich lerne Deutsch sprechen). There are also verbs that require 'zu' after an object (Ich bitte dich zu kommen). Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, etc.) only use the infinitive without 'zu'. Verbs like 'anfangen', 'vergessen', 'versuchen' always take 'zu' with the infinitive. Additionally, when the infinitive is the subject of the sentence, the construction 'es ist' + 'zu' is used (Es ist wichtig, Deutsch zu lernen) or the noun (Das Lernen macht Spaß).

Avoid translating the Spanish gerund literally; look for the appropriate German structure depending on the main verb.

title: Modal verbs for assumptions (muss, könnte, mag) / Modal verbs for deduction (muss, könnte, mag)
bridge: In Spanish, we use periphrases like 'debe de ser' or adverbs like 'quizás' with the subjunctive to express deduction. In German, the modal verbs 'müssen', 'können', and 'mögen' are used directly with the infinitive to indicate different degrees of certainty. A common mistake is using 'sollen' for deductions (it is incorrect) and confusing 'müssen' with obligation, when in a deduction context it means 'probably'. Additionally, the word order is different: the modal verb goes in second position and the main verb at the end.
rule: To express assumptions in German (level B1), modal verbs are used with an infinitive at the end of the sentence. **Müssen** indicates a logical deduction based on evidence (equivalent to 'debe de' in Spanish). **Können** expresses a possibility (equivalent to 'podría' or 'puede que'). **Mögen** (in this use) expresses a more remote possibility or with reservations (equivalent to 'puede que', but less certain). The structure is: subject + conjugated modal in present + (complements) + infinitive at the end. Example: 'Er muss zu Hause sein' (He must be at home). The subjunctive II of the modal can also be used for greater uncertainty: 'Er könnte zu Hause sein' (He could be at home). With the perfect tense, the perfect infinitive is used: 'Er muss das gemacht haben' (He must have done it). It is important not to use 'sollen' for deductions (only for hearsay).

title: Relative clauses (defining and non-defining)
bridge: In Spanish, we distinguish between explanatory relative clauses (with commas) and specifying ones (without commas), using 'que', 'quien', 'cual', etc. In German, the structure is different: the conjugated verb goes at the end of the relative clause, and the relative pronouns (der, die, das, etc.) agree in gender and number with the antecedent, but their case depends on their function within the subordinate clause. Additionally, in German, the relative pronoun cannot be omitted (as is sometimes done in Spanish with 'que' or 'donde'), nor can prepositions be placed at the end as in Spanish; the preposition comes before the relative pronoun.
rule: Relative clauses in German are introduced by relative pronouns derived from the definite article (der, die, das, etc.) and agree in gender and number with the noun they refer to, but their case (nominative, accusative, dative, or genitive) depends on their function within the subordinate clause. The conjugated verb always comes at the end of the relative clause. Defining (specifying) clauses do not have commas and restrict meaning; explanatory (non-defining) clauses are set off by commas and add extra information. For referring to people, 'wer' (who) can also be used in a general sense. In the genitive case, 'dessen' (whose/his) and 'deren' (whose/her/their) are used. When the relative pronoun is preceded by a preposition, the preposition is placed before the pronoun (e.g., 'mit dem', 'für die'). The relative pronoun cannot be omitted, unlike in Spanish.

title: / Präteritum (Konjunktiv II) – Unreal wishes
bridge: In Spanish, we use the subjunctive (quisiera, pudiera, tuviera) to express unreal wishes. In German, the equivalent form is the Konjunktiv II, which is constructed with 'würde + infinitive' or with modal and auxiliary verbs in the Präteritum. The English 'wish' is not translated literally; in German, we use 'würde' or the past Konjunktiv II to indicate that the situation is hypothetical or contrary to reality.
rule: To express unreal wishes in German (equivalent to 'wish + past' in English), the Konjunktiv II is used. This is formed in two main ways: 1) With the auxiliary 'würde' followed by the infinitive of the main verb: 'Ich würde gerne mehr Zeit haben' (I would like to have more time). 2) With the modal verbs 'können', 'dürfen', 'müssen' and the auxiliaries 'haben' and 'sein' in their Präteritum form (with umlaut if necessary): 'Ich hätte gern ein neues Auto' (I would like a new car), 'Ich könnte dir helfen' (I could help you). The Konjunktiv II of common verbs is also used to express wishes: 'Ich wäre gern reich' (I would like to be rich), 'Ich ginge gern ins Kino' (I would like to go to the cinema). In spoken language, 'würde + infinitive' is more common, except for modal verbs and 'haben', 'sein', 'werden', where the simple form is preferred. The typical structure for unreal wishes is: 'Ich wünschte + würde/past' or simply the Konjunktiv II. Example: 'Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit' (I wish I had more time).

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish the present subjunctive ('tenga') is used after 'ojalá', and students tend to translate 'wünsche' as 'ojalá' using the present tense. 'Ich wünsche' indicates a real wish in the present, not an unreal one.

title: Expressing habits in the past / Expressing past habits
bridge: In Spanish, we use the preterite imperfect ('yo jugaba', 'solía jugar') to express past habits. In German, there is no specific tense for past habits; the Präteritum or Perfekt is used, often accompanied by words like 'früher', 'immer', or 'manchmal' to indicate a habitual action. A common mistake is translating 'solía + infinitive' directly as 'ich pflegte zu + infinitive', which sounds very formal and uncommon. It is more natural to use the past tense with frequency adverbs.
rule: To express past habits in German, the Präteritum (for repeated actions in the past) or Perfekt (more colloquial) is normally used, along with temporal adverbs such as 'früher' (before), 'immer' (always), 'oft' (often), or 'manchmal' (sometimes). The structure is: subject + verb in past tense (second position) + complement + adverb. The construction 'pflegte zu + infinitive' (used to) also exists but is rare in everyday language; it is preferred in literary texts. The verb 'pflegen' is conjugated in Präteritum as: ich pflegte, du pflegtest, er pflegte, etc. For B1 level, it is sufficient to master the use of adverbs and the past tense.

title: Purpose, cause and result / Purpose, cause and result
bridge: In Spanish, you use 'para que', 'porque', 'así que' with subjunctive or indicative. In German, subordinating conjunctions (um...zu, damit, weil, denn, sodass) change the word order: the conjugated verb goes at the end in subordinate clauses (except with 'denn' and 'deshalb', which maintain normal order). Many Spanish speakers forget to place the verb at the end or confuse 'weil' (cause) with 'denn' (cause with normal order).
rule:
To express purpose (Zweck):
- 'um...zu' + infinitive: used when the subject of the main clause is the same as in the subordinate clause. Example: 'Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Berlin zu arbeiten.' (I am learning German to work in Berlin).
- 'damit' + subordinate clause with verb at the end: used when the subject is different. Example: 'Ich lerne Deutsch, damit du stolz bist.' (I am learning German so that you are proud).

To express cause (Ursache):
- 'weil' (because): subordinate clause with verb at the end. Example: 'Ich bin müde, weil ich viel gearbeitet habe.' (I am tired because I worked a lot).
- 'denn' (for, because): coordinate clause with normal order. Example: 'Ich bin müde, denn ich habe viel gearbeitet.' (Note: 'denn' is not used at the beginning of the sentence).
- 'da' (as, since): subordinate clause with verb at the end, used when the cause is known or important. Example: 'Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.'

To express result (Folge):
- 'sodass' / 'so dass' (so that, with the result that): subordinate clause with verb at the end. Example: 'Es regnete, sodass wir zu Hause blieben.'
- 'deshalb' / 'deswegen' (therefore, that's why): coordinate clause with normal order; the verb is in second position but the phrase can start with 'deshalb' + verb + subject. Example: 'Es regnete, deshalb blieben wir zu Hause.'

Remember: with subordinate clauses (weil, da, damit, sodass), the conjugated verb goes at the end. With 'denn' and 'deshalb', the order is normal (subject + verb).

title: Separable Verbs / Verbos separables
bridge: In German, many verbs have a prefix that separates in the present and imperfect tenses and moves to the end of the sentence, which has no direct equivalent in Spanish. While in Spanish we say 'apagar' (a single verb), in German it is 'ausschalten' (aus + schalten), and in a main clause the 'aus' jumps to the end: 'Ich schalte das Licht aus'. This often confuses Spanish speakers because they expect the full verb together. Additionally, in subordinate clauses the verb (with its prefix) goes to the end, and in the past participle the prefix remains attached but with 'ge-' inserted: 'ausgeschaltet'.
rule: Separable verbs (trennbare Verben) have a prefix that is a preposition or adverb (an, auf, aus, ein, mit, nach, vor, zu, etc.). In the present indicative and imperative, the prefix separates and is placed at the end of the main clause. The conjugated verb occupies the second position. In the subordinate clause (with 'dass', 'weil', etc.), the conjugated verb (with its attached prefix) goes at the end. In the past participle, 'ge-' is added between the prefix and the verb: 'aufmachen' → 'aufgemacht'. In the infinitive with 'zu', the 'zu' is placed between the prefix and the verb: 'aufzumachen'. Separable verbs are very common in everyday language. Examples: 'anfangen' (to begin), 'aufstehen' (to get up), 'einkaufen' (to shop), 'fernsehen' (to watch TV), 'mitkommen' (to come along). Some prefixes like 'be-', 'ver-', 'er-' are inseparable, and their verbs do not separate. It is important to learn separable verbs as vocabulary units and practice the placement of the prefix.

title: Quantifiers (kaum, reichlich) / Advanced quantifiers (apenas, abundante)
bridge: In Spanish we use words like 'apenas', 'poco', 'suficiente' or 'un montón de', but in German these quantifiers have their own nuances and constructions, such as 'kaum' (apenas) which is used with verbs in normal position, not at the end, and 'reichlich' (abundante) which is used in formal contexts. A typical error is to translate 'apenas tengo' literally as 'ich habe kaum' instead of, for example, 'ich habe kaum etwas' (I hardly have anything), or to confuse 'einige' (some) with 'ein paar' (a couple).
rule: In German, advanced quantifiers include: kaum (hardly, almost nothing), reichlich (abundant, sufficient in quantity), eine Menge (a lot of, a good number of), ziemlich viel (quite a lot), zu wenig (too little), genug (enough). They are used as adjectives or adverbs: typically with nouns in the accusative case, or as adverbs without modifying the noun. 'Kaum' is usually placed before the conjugated verb in position 2 (since it is a frequency adverb) and modifies the verb or the noun: 'Ich habe kaum Zeit' (I hardly have time). 'Reichlich' is more formal and can mean 'abundant' or 'more than enough': 'Wir haben reichlich Platz' (We have more than enough space). 'Genug' and 'zu wenig' are used after the noun or as adverbs: 'Ich habe genug Geld' or 'Ich habe Geld genug' (less common). Exceptions: 'kaum' is not combined with 'nicht' (you don’t say 'nicht kaum'), and 'einige' is used in the plural, while 'ein paar' is also used with plural nouns. At B1 level, it’s important to know that 'kaum' implies an almost zero quantity, and 'wenig' expresses 'little' but not as extreme.

common_error.explanation: The error is to translate the Spanish double negative ('apenas no tengo') literally. In German, 'kaum' already expresses a weak negation (almost nothing), so it cannot be combined with 'nicht'. The correct form is simply 'ich habe kaum Geld' (I hardly have any money) or use 'fast kein' (almost none), which is an equivalent alternative but with a different structure. Spanish speakers tend to add 'nicht' because in some regions Spanish uses 'apenas no tengo', but in German this is an error. To avoid this mistake, remember that 'kaum' already includes a negative sense, and if you want to negate it completely, use 'fast kein' plus the noun.

examples.original: Hast du genug gegessen?
examples.phonetic: hast duː ˈɡeːnuːk ɡəˈɡɛsən
examples.translation: Have you eaten enough?
examples.note: As an adverb, 'genug' is used without a noun. Here it modifies the verb 'gegessen'.

examples.original: Er hat zu wenig Schlaf bekommen.
examples.phonetic: eːɐ̯ hat t͡suː ˈviːnɪç ʃlaːf bəˈkɔmən
examples.translation: He got far too little sleep.
examples.note: 'Zu wenig' with a countable noun. In Spanish we would say 'poco sueño', but German needs 'zu' to mark excessive lack.

title: Verb + Infinitive or Gerund? // Verb + infinitive or gerund
bridge: In Spanish, we use both the infinitive and the gerund after certain verbs (e.g., 'sigo estudiando', 'evito hablar'). In German, the gerund barely exists; the infinitive (often with 'zu') or the 'am ... sein' structure is used for ongoing actions. A common trap is translating the Spanish gerund literally: 'estoy comiendo' cannot be said *'ich bin essend'*, but rather 'ich bin am Essen' or simply 'ich esse'. However, most German verb patterns require the infinitive: 'ich versuche zu schlafen' (I try to sleep) and not 'ich versuche schlafend'.
rule: In German (level B1), verbs that in Spanish are followed by the gerund (such as 'sigo aprendiendo' or 'continúo trabajando') are expressed with: 1) Infinitive with 'zu' after verbs like 'versuchen' (to try), 'hoffen' (to hope), 'planen' (to plan), 'empfehlen' (to recommend), 'vergessen' (to forget), 'anfangen' (to start), 'aufhören' (to stop). 2) Infinitive without 'zu' after modal verbs (können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen) and after 'werden' (future). 3) The construction 'am + infinitive + sein' to express an ongoing action ('ich bin am Kochen' = I am cooking). 4) In subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb goes at the end: 'Ich hoffe, dass ich bald schlafen kann.' Be careful: do not use the gerund in German; it does not exist as a verb form. There are also verbs that require 'zu' + infinitive and in Spanish are constructed with a preposition + infinitive ('sich darauf freuen, ... zu' = to look forward to ...).

concept_examples.text: Ich versuche, früh aufzustehen.
concept_examples.translation: I try to get up early.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪç fɛɐ̯ˈzuːxə, fʁyː ˈaʊ̯fˌt͡suːʃteːən.

concept_examples.text: Wir haben aufgehört, laut zu reden.
concept_examples.translation: We have stopped talking loudly.
concept_examples.phonetic: vɪʁ ˈhaːbən ˈaʊ̯fɡəhøːɐ̯t, laʊ̯t t͡su ˈʁeːdən.

concept_examples.text: Er hofft, den Zug zu erreichen.
concept_examples.translation: He hopes to catch the train.
concept_examples.phonetic: eːɐ̯ hɔft, deːn t͡suːk t͡su ɛɐ̯ˈʁaɪ̯çən.

concept_examples.text: Sie ist am Kochen.
concept_examples.translation: She is cooking.
concept_examples.phonetic: ziː ɪst am ˈkɔxən.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'intento dormir' uses the infinitive without a preposition, but in German the verb 'versuchen' requires the particle 'zu' before the infinitive. The error comes from directly transferring from Spanish, where there is no equivalent particle. To avoid it, remember that many German verbs (such as versuchen, hoffen, planen) need 'zu' + infinitive in the same sentence, even if the subject is the same.

examples.original: Ich hoffe, dich bald zu sehen.
examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈhɔfə, dɪç balt t͡su ˈzeːən.
examples.translation: I hope to see you soon.
examples.note: The verb 'hoffen' (to hope) is followed by 'zu' + infinitive, even if there is no comma in short phrases.

examples.original: Vergiss nicht, die Tür zu schließen.
examples.phonetic: fɛɐ̯ˈɡɪs nɪçt, diː tyːɐ̯ t͡su ˈʃliːsən.
examples.translation: Don't forget to close the door.
examples.note: With 'vergessen' (to forget) we use 'nicht' + 'zu' + infinitive to express 'not forgetting to do something'.

examples.original: Er hat angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen.
examples.phonetic: eːɐ̯ hat ˈanɡəfaŋən, dɔɪ̯tʃ t͡su ˈlɛʁnən.
examples.translation: He has started to learn German.
examples.note: 'Anfangen' (to start) requires 'zu' + infinitive; in Spanish we use 'a' + infinitive, but here there is no preposition.

examples.original: Wir empfehlen dir, mehr zu üben.
examples.phonetic: vɪʁ ɛmˈpfeːlən diːɐ̯, meːɐ̯ t͡su ˈyːbən.
examples.translation: We recommend you to practice more.
examples.note: After 'empfehlen' (to recommend) 'zu' + infinitive is used, even if the object is a person.

examples.original: Ich kann gut schwimmen.
examples.phonetic: ɪç kan guːt ˈʃvɪmən.
examples.translation: I can swim well.
examples.note: The modal 'können' is always followed by an infinitive without 'zu'.

examples.original: Du musst morgen früh aufstehen.
examples.phonetic: duː mʊst ˈmɔʁɡən fʁyː ˈaʊ̯fˌʃteːən.
examples.translation: You must get up early tomorrow.
examples.note: The verb 'müssen' (to have to) combines with an infinitive without 'zu'.

examples.original: Wir wollen heute Abend ausgehen.
examples.phonetic: vɪʁ ˈvɔlən ˈhɔɪ̯tə ˈaːbənt ˈaʊ̯sɡeːən.
examples.translation: We want to go out tonight.
examples.note: The modal 'wollen' (to want) is also used without 'zu'.

examples.original: Soll ich das Fenster öffnen?
examples.phonetic: zɔl ɪç das ˈfɛnstɐ ˈœfnən.
examples.translation: Should I open the window?
examples.note: In questions with 'sollen' (should) the infinitive is placed at the end, without 'zu'.

levels.label: am + Infinitiv + sein / Ersatz für Gerundium

examples.original: Ich bin am Arbeiten.
examples.phonetic: ɪç bɪn am ˈaʁbaɪ̯tən.
examples.translation: I am working.
examples.note: This construction expresses an ongoing action, similar to the Spanish gerund.

examples.original: Sie ist am Telefonieren.
examples.phonetic: ziː ɪst am teːləˈfoːnɪʁən.
examples.translation: She is talking on the phone.
examples.note: It is very common in colloquial German, especially in the north.

examples.original: Wir sind am Packen.
examples.phonetic: vɪʁ zɪnt am ˈpakən.
examples.translation: We are packing our suitcases.
examples.note: It is used with verbs that express activities; it is not possible with all verbs.

examples.original: Er ist am Einschlafen.
examples.phonetic: eːɐ̯ ɪst am ˈaɪ̯nʃlaːfən.
examples.translation: He is falling asleep.
examples.note: The separable verb prefix can be added, but the form is 'am + infinitive'.

title: Nullartikel und generischer Gebrauch / Generic use and zero article
bridge: In Spanish, we often use the definite or indefinite article where German omits it. For example, we say 'Me gusta el pan' or 'El agua es vida', but in German, the article is omitted in generic uses and with uncountable nouns ('Ich mag Brot', 'Wasser ist Leben'). This difference is key: German uses the 'zero article' (Nullartikel) to express generalities, while Spanish tends to use 'el/la/los/las'. It is also important to learn when German uses an article in contexts where Spanish does not, such as with professions or nationalities.
rule: The zero article (Nullartikel) in German is used in the following main cases: 1) Plural nouns in a generic sense: 'Kinder spielen gern' (Children like to play). 2) Uncountable or abstract nouns in a general sense: 'Ich trinke Kaffee' (I drink coffee), 'Liebe ist wichtig' (Love is important). 3) With names of countries, cities, and continents in the neuter gender: 'Deutschland liegt in Europa'. Exception: countries with an article (die Schweiz, die Türkei, der Iran) always take an article. 4) With professions, nationalities, and religions after 'sein' or 'werden': 'Er ist Lehrer' (He is a teacher), 'Sie ist Spanierin' (She is Spanish). 5) In phrases with 'ohne' (without) and 'als' (as): 'ohne Zucker', 'als Kind' (as a child). NOTE: When the noun is specific or determined (by context, adjective, etc.), the definite or indefinite article is used. For example: 'Ich trinke den Kaffee' (the specific coffee), 'ein Lehrer' (a teacher, one of many). For B1 level, mastering the zero article is essential for talking about preferences, habits, and generalities.

concept_examples.text: Ich mag Brot.
concept_examples.translation: I like bread.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪç maːk bʁoːt

concept_examples.text: Wasser ist Leben.
concept_examples.translation: Water is life.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈvasɐ ɪst ˈleːbən

concept_examples.text: Kinder spielen gern im Park.
concept_examples.translation: Children like to play in the park.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈkɪndɐ ˈʃpiːlən ɡɛʁn ɪm paʁk

concept_examples.text: Er ist Lehrer von Beruf.
concept_examples.translation: He is a teacher by profession.
concept_examples.phonetic: eːɐ ɪst ˈleːʁɐ fɔn bəˈʁuːf

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we say 'me gusta el pan' with a definite article, and Spanish speakers transfer this structure to German. However, to express a general preference (without referring to a specific bread), German uses the zero article. If you say 'Ich mag das Brot', you are talking about a specific bread (for example, the one on the table). To avoid this error, ask yourself: am I talking about something in general or something specific? If it is general, omit the article.

levels.label: Nullartikel bei unzählbaren Nomen und Abstrakta
levels.translation: Zero article with uncountable and abstract nouns

examples.original: Ich trinke Kaffee zum Frühstück.
examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈtʁɪŋkə ˈkafeː t͡sʊm ˈfʁyːʃtʏk
examples.translation: I drink coffee for breakfast.
examples.note: In general, the article is omitted with uncountable nouns like Kaffee, Wasser, Milch, if they are not determined.

examples.original: Liebe ist das Wichtigste im Leben.
examples.phonetic: ˈliːbə ɪst das ˈvɪçtɪçstə ɪm ˈleːbən
examples.translation: Love is the most important thing in life.
examples.note: Abstract nouns (Liebe, Glück, Zeit) also use the zero article in a general sense.

examples.original: Hast du Hunger?
examples.phonetic: hast duː ˈhʊŋɐ
examples.translation: Are you hungry?
examples.note: With feelings or states (Hunger, Durst, Angst) the zero article is used; it is not said 'un hambre'.

levels.label: Nullartikel bei pluralen Nomen und Ländernamen
levels.translation: Zero article with plurals and names of countries

examples.original: Äpfel sind gesund.
examples.phonetic: ˈɛpfəl zɪnt ɡəˈzʊnt
examples.translation: Apples are healthy.
examples.note: Generic plurals do not take the definite article; in Spanish we use 'las manzanas'.

examples.original: Deutschland liegt in Europa.
examples.phonetic: ˈdɔʏtʃlant liːkt ɪn ɔɪˈʁoːpa
examples.translation: Germany is in Europe.
examples.note: Most countries (neuter) do not take an article, unlike Spain which does take 'das spanien'? No, but remember exceptions.

examples.original: Ich war in Italien.
examples.phonetic: ɪç vaʁ ɪn ʔiˈtaːli̯ən
examples.translation: I was in Italy.
examples.note: With neuter countries, the preposition 'in' is used without an article; but with countries that take an article, it is said 'in der Schweiz'.

levels.label: Nullartikel nach sein, werden, als und ohne
levels.translation: Zero article after sein, werden, als and ohne

examples.original: Sie ist Ärztin.
examples.phonetic: ziː ɪst ˈɛːɐ̯t͡stɪn
examples.translation: She is a doctor.
examples.note: No article is used with professions after 'sein' (to be). In Spanish we sometimes say 'es una médica', but in German it is incorrect.

examples.original: Er wird Ingenieur.
examples.phonetic: eːɐ vɪʁt ɪnʒeˈni̯øːɐ
examples.translation: He is becoming an engineer.
examples.note: With 'werden' (to become) the article is also omitted.

examples.original: Als Kind habe ich viel gespielt.
examples.phonetic: als kɪnt ˈhaːbə ɪç fiːl ɡəˈʃpiːlt
examples.translation: As a child, I played a lot.
examples.note: The preposition 'als' (as) requires the zero article with undetermined nouns.

examples.original: Ich trinke Tee ohne Zucker.
examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈtʁɪŋkə teː ˈoːnə ˈt͡sʊkɐ
examples.translation: I drink tea without sugar.
examples.note: After 'ohne' (without) the article is omitted.
